title: Assessing psychological, neural, and AI-based representational geometries across multiple similarity properties
text:
← Research

Status: Active — under review for publication
Research area: Perception





An illustrative comparison of three ways of organizing objects: people’s judgments, patterns of brain activity, and AI models.





Think about an apple, a tennis ball, and a strawberry. An apple might seem similar to a tennis ball because both are round, but closer to a strawberry if you are thinking about food. Ask which objects have a similar color, which you like, or which seem frightening, and the groupings may change again. In this project, I ask how these different ways of comparing things relate to the way our brains and artificial intelligence systems organize the world. Participants compared 280 objects from 40 categories using several kinds of judgments: general similarity, shape, color, whether something is alive, preference, scariness, and dissimilarity. Rather than looking at each object on its own, I use these comparisons to build a kind of map of relationships: objects judged to be similar belong closer together, while objects judged to be different belong farther apart. I then compare the structure of those maps with patterns of brain activity measured using fMRI in 11 regions of the cortex, and with representations produced by artificial neural networks and other computational models. The aim is to understand which relationships these different systems share, and which depend on the question we ask. For example, organizing objects by their appearance may reveal a different picture from organizing them by how we feel about them. Another important part of the work is understanding the limits of our measurements. Brain recordings and human judgments are not perfectly consistent, so a weak match between two maps does not automatically mean that the brain and behavior are organized in completely different ways. By taking that uncertainty into account, I aim to make comparisons between people, brains, and AI more informative about what they do—and do not—have in common.






How similar do objects seem when we compare their appearance, meaning, or the feelings they evoke?



How do patterns of fMRI activity relate to those judgments across different brain regions?



Which relationships also appear in artificial neural networks and other computational models?





The comparison method is called Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA). The manuscript provides the technical details, including measurement reliability and the limits that noise places on comparisons with brain activity.

title: Neural Dynamics of Motion Repulsion
text:
← Research

Status: Active — analyses ongoing; manuscript in preparation
Research areas: Perception · Working Memory





EEG can be examined around viewing, remembering, and reporting motion.





A visual illusion tells us that our experience is not a simple copy of what reaches our eyes. But a person’s final answer cannot tell us exactly when the distortion arose. Did it begin while they were seeing the stimulus, develop while they held it in memory, or emerge as they decided what to report? This project takes the motion-repulsion question into EEG, which records the changing electrical activity detectable at the scalp. Participants view moving-dot displays and report what they perceived, allowing me to compare brain activity from trials where two directions seemed to move farther apart with trials where they appeared to pull together or showed relatively little bias. Because EEG follows activity over time, it provides a way to examine different stages of the task rather than only the final response. I look both at brief changes associated with task events and at patterns of rhythmic activity, and use methods that test whether information about the task can be distinguished across patterns of signals. The aim is to understand when interactions between motion representations become apparent and how those interactions relate to memory and decision-making. Analyses are ongoing, so this page presents the questions and approach rather than a settled account of the neural mechanism. Together with the behavioral experiments, the project asks how an apparently small distortion of motion can reveal the steps through which the brain constructs what we experience.



The analysis combines event-related responses, changes in rhythmic brain activity, and multivariate decoding using the TIMEGAL toolbox. These approaches offer complementary ways of asking what changes over time and what information is present in the recorded signals.



Brian Odegaard, Andreas Keil, and Alejandro Santos-Mayo. Perception, Artificial Intelligence, Metacognition, and Consciousness Lab, University of Florida.



A public manuscript or repository is not yet available.

title: Sense of Agency, Automation and Videogames: A new framework for Human Machine Interactions
text:
← Research

Status: Completed — MSc thesis
Research areas: Interactive Cognition · Consciousness · Decision-Making





An action can involve a person, an automated system, and an outcome in either a physical or a virtual setting.





When you press a button and a character jumps, it usually feels as though you made the jump happen. That feeling is an example of a sense of agency: the experience that an action or its outcome belongs to you. But what happens when a system takes over part of the action? A game might help you aim, a machine might choose how to carry out an instruction, or an automated system might decide what happens next. In this project, I explored how people understand their own role in actions that involve both human choices and machine assistance. I combined behavioral experiments with theoretical work to compare physical interactions with the richer possibilities offered by video games. The key idea is that control has several levels: we can choose a goal, choose an action, or control the movements that carry it out. Handing over one of those levels may feel very different from handing over another. In the experimental work, high-level automation was associated with a reduced sense of agency. The qualitative analysis of games raised a different possibility: assistance can sometimes help players achieve their intentions and thereby support a feeling of agency. These are different kinds of evidence, so the contrast is a question to investigate rather than proof that games reverse the effects of automation. More broadly, the project helped establish my interest in using games as environments where we can study how intentions, feedback, and control come together to shape experience.



Games allow researchers to vary a person’s choices, the assistance offered by a system, and the feedback that follows. That makes them useful for studying control in situations that go beyond a single button press in a laboratory.



École Normale Supérieure / Institut Jean Nicod — Action Lab. Supervisors: Valérian Chambon and Elisabeth Pacherie.

title: Cognitive and Metacognitive Constraints on Motion Repulsion
text:
← Research

Status: Active — manuscript in preparation
Research areas: Perception · Working Memory · Metacognition





Nearby motion directions can appear more widely separated.





Imagine watching two groups of dots moving in slightly different directions. Even when the directions are fairly close, they can appear to be pushed farther apart. This illusion is called motion repulsion, and I use it to ask a broader question: how do seeing, remembering, paying attention, and judging our own experience influence one another? In a series of experiments, participants watch moving dots, keep information in mind, and report a motion direction. I vary how much they need to remember, where their attention is directed, and which movement they are later asked to report. I also ask how confident they are, because being affected by an illusion and knowing that your perception is uncertain are not necessarily the same thing. Instead of reducing the illusion to one number, I look at several aspects of the response: how far the reported direction shifts, how often it shifts away from rather than toward the other direction, and how precisely the movement is remembered. The results so far suggest that motion repulsion can remain robust even when memory demands and attentional conditions change. That does not mean attention and memory never matter; it means that giving people fewer resources does not simply make the interaction between motion representations disappear. The ongoing work asks whether people can recognize these distortions through their confidence, and whether that awareness depends on which movement they are trying to recall.



The observations described here are preliminary. The ongoing confidence experiments examine what people can tell us about the distortions in their own perception.
Parts of this research have been presented at the Vision Sciences Society and the University of Florida.



Brian Odegaard and the Artificial Intelligence, Metacognition, and Consciousness Lab, University of Florida. Undergraduate and student collaborators contributed across the behavioral experiments.



Related conference abstract: Task-irrelevant motion information modulates working memory representations. Journal of Vision, 24(10), 1433.

title: Prestimulus Neural Activity and Subsequent Conscious Perception
text:
← Research

Status: Active — preregistered secondary analyses
Research areas: Consciousness · Perception · Decision-Making





The project asks whether activity before a stimulus is informative about later conscious perception.





We often think of seeing as something that starts when an object appears. Yet the brain is already active before that moment, and the same incoming information may arrive when it is in very different states. In this project, I ask whether those earlier states help explain why a stimulus enters conscious experience on one occasion but not another. Rather than collecting a new experiment from scratch, the work uses large, openly available brain-imaging datasets to ask new questions about activity recorded before a stimulus appeared. The initial analyses focus on fMRI, which measures changes related to blood oxygenation, and examine both activity in particular brain regions and how regions work together. An important comparison is between experiments where people explicitly report what they saw and experiments that reduce or remove that report. Saying that you saw something also involves making a decision and producing an action, so separating those demands helps clarify which signals might relate to the experience itself. The project is guided by competing theories of consciousness: the aim is to ask whether they make distinguishable predictions about the state from which a conscious perceptual experience emerges. Hypotheses and analysis choices are specified in advance wherever possible, so that the tests are less shaped by whichever patterns happen to appear in the data. Supported by a 2026 Consciousness Commons Award, the work brings together questions about perception, conscious experience, and the value of reusing open scientific data.



Supported by the Consciousness Commons Award (2026). Funder: Templeton World Charity Foundation. Partner: DataCite.
The project uses preregistered secondary analyses of open neuroimaging datasets. Public preregistration and analysis-repository links will be added when available.



Nicolas Comay, Nicolas Bruno, Mathis Immertreu, Sharif Kronemer, and Pablo Barttfeld.

title: Not so fast! Comparing the neural markers of self-generated urgency regimes in voluntary actions
text:
← Research

Status: Completed — MSc dissertation, awarded Distinction
Research areas: Decision-Making





Two sources of urgency can lead to the same question: when should I act?





Imagine waiting to cross a street. Sometimes a signal tells you when to move; at other times, you have to decide for yourself when you are ready. Both situations involve a decision about timing, but the pressure to act can come from different places. In this project, I investigated how the brain prepares a voluntary action and how that preparation changes when people act quickly because they have been instructed to, or because they choose to. One useful way to think about a decision is as a process of gathering information until there is enough to act. But information is not the only thing that matters: a growing feeling that it is time to make a choice may also push us toward action. I used EEG, a method that records small electrical signals from sensors on the scalp, to study how these processes unfold over time. Rather than treating the moment of movement as the whole decision, I looked at the activity leading up to it. The broader question was whether different sources of urgency rely on similar preparation or change the way a decision develops. title: Not so fast! Comparing the neural markers of self-generated urgency regimes in voluntary actions
text: Imagine waiting to cross a street. Sometimes a signal tells you when to move; at other times, you have to decide for yourself when you are ready. Both situations involve a decision about timing, but the pressure to act can come from different places. In this project, I investigated how the brain prepares a voluntary action and how that preparation changes when people act quickly because they have been instructed to, or because they choose to. One useful way to think about a decision is as a process of gathering information until there is enough to act. But information is not the only thing that matters: a growing feeling that it is time to make a choice may also push us toward action. I used EEG, a method that records small electrical signals from sensors on the scalp, to study how these processes unfold over time. Rather than treating the moment of movement as the whole decision, I looked at the activity leading up to it. The broader question was whether different sources of urgency rely on similar preparation or change the way a decision develops. This work formed my MSc dissertation and gave me experience taking an EEG experiment from recording through early stages of cleaning and analyzing the signals. It also helped shape my interest in connecting the experience of choosing an action with the brain processes that make that choice possible.
